item.title: Tax crimes make up 86% of FFIU case value as MPs question tracking of drug money
item.description: Tax crimes accounted for approximately 86 percent of the transaction value linked to case dissemination reports by Fiji’s Financial Intelligence Unit (FFIU) in 2024, while MPs have raised concerns over whether Fiji has the capacity to effectively trace money linked to drug trafficking and organised crime. item.content:encoded:
Tax crimes accounted for approximately 86 percent of the transaction value linked to case dissemination reports by Fiji’s Financial Intelligence Unit (FFIU) in 2024, while MPs have raised concerns over whether Fiji has the capacity to effectively trace money linked to drug trafficking and organised crime.

The FFIU functions as both a regulatory body and a national financial intelligence unit to protect Fiji's financial system from criminal abuse.

Opposition MP Rinesh Sharma raised this issue during Parliament’s debate on the Standing Committee on Economic Affairs’ review of the FFIU’s 2024 Annual Report.

Sharma says tax crimes accounted for 26 percent of case dissemination reports by number, but represented approximately 86 percent of the transaction value associated with those reports.

Insert: Sharma - Every scam is every family being robbed Sept 28

He says this highlights the significant financial exposure associated with tax-related offences and the need for stronger analysis and enforcement.

He has proposed a series of measures to strengthen Fiji’s ability to monitor and trace money linked to financial and organised crime.

Sharma is calling for amendments to the Financial Transactions Reporting Act to cover emerging areas including virtual assets and cryptocurrency exchanges, mobile money, digital wallets, gold and precious metal dealers, motor vehicle dealers and other high-value traders.

He says the amendments should also establish a beneficial ownership register, increase penalties and require agencies receiving financial intelligence to report back to the Fiji Financial Intelligence Unit on the outcome of referrals within 90 days.

Sharma is also calling for increased funding for the FFIU, including doubling its analytical capacity to clear the backlog of suspicious transaction reports within 12 months.

Sharma is further calling for greater use of the Proceeds of Crime Act and the introduction of unexplained wealth orders to help trace and recover proceeds of crime.

He says recovered funds should be directed towards areas including drug rehabilitation, HIV response and frontline policing.

Sharma also wants stronger supervision of high-risk professionals, including lawyers, accountants and real estate agents, with on-site examinations at least once every three years and greater use of administrative penalties.

He says Fiji also needs to strengthen its borders by improving cash declaration measures at airports and ports and increasing scanning and surveillance at marinas and remote jetties.

Sharma also questioned whether Fiji’s financial intelligence system is sufficiently equipped to follow the proceeds of organised crime and drug trafficking.

He referred to major drug seizures and says proceeds from illicit activities can potentially move through bank accounts, businesses, vehicles, land and property.

Sharma says Parliament is unable to establish how many investigations, prosecutions, convictions and asset recoveries resulted from intelligence produced by the FFIU.

Meanwhile, the FFIU received 559 suspicious transaction reports in 2024 and analysed 304, leaving 255 reports outstanding.

Sharma says the unit’s capacity needs to be strengthened so the outstanding reports can be cleared within 12 months.

He is also calling for stronger links between the National Intelligence Bureau, FICA, the Director of Public Prosecutions and the Fiji Police Force through a shared case-management system.

Sharma has proposed amendments to the Financial Transactions Reporting Act to address emerging areas including virtual assets, cryptocurrency exchanges, mobile money, digital wallets, gold and precious metal dealers, motor vehicle dealers and other high-value traders.

He also called for greater use of proceeds-of-crime legislation, unexplained wealth orders and stronger supervision of high-risk sectors.

Opposition MP Faiyaz Koya also raised concerns over the growing complexity of financial crime, including the use of cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin.

Koya says additional funding, training and capacity building will be needed to ensure the FFIU can provide the intelligence required by Police and other agencies dealing with transnational crime and drug-related offences.

While presenting the committee’s review, Chair and Assistant Minister in the Office of the Prime Minister Sakiusa Tubuna says the central concern was that intelligence generated by the FFIU was not always translating into the outcomes being sought.

Tubuna says the committee found there was no systematic feedback showing what happened to intelligence after it was disseminated, including whether it resulted in investigations, prosecutions, convictions or asset recoveries.

He says stronger coordination between the FFIU and recipient agencies, together with a formal feedback mechanism, is needed to ensure intelligence contributes to enforcement action.

The motion to note the review of the FFIU 2024 Annual Report was agreed to unanimously in parliament.

item.title: King of Tonga in tears after meeting WOWS Kids founders’ daughter battling cancer
item.description: Tears filled the King of Tonga’s eyes as he left Tae Kami’s family home after an emotional meeting with her while she battled terminal cancer, just weeks before his coronation. This was highlighted by WOWS Kids co-founders Taholo Kami and Sina Kami during Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan.
item.content:encoded:
Tears filled the King of Tonga’s eyes as he left Tae Kami’s family home after an emotional meeting with her while she battled terminal cancer, just weeks before his coronation.

This was highlighted by WOWS Kids co-founders Taholo Kami and Sina Kami during Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan.

Taholo says Tae believed the King’s unexpected visit was the reason she was still alive, so she could meet the King of Tonga before meeting the King of Kings.

Insert: Sina Kami on King of Tonga's visit 28th Sept

Tae's Father shares despite being in severe pain that day, Tae was determined to perform a song for the King as she took the time to tune her guitar before telling the King she could not attend his coronation but wanted to give him the song as her present.

Taholo says the moment was significant because it showed the human side of the new King and his connection with the people of Tonga.

He says Tae’s condition had deteriorated in her final weeks, with severe waves of pain requiring strong medication.

He says music became one of the ways they helped her through the pain, with Tae sometimes simply asking him to sing.

item.title: Rod Stewart confirms final tour after heart procedure and health scares
item.description: Rod Stewart has announced that his next tour will be his last. The 81-year-old singer has been touring since the early 1960s, when he set out across Europe with a harmonica – and ended up getting deported from Spain for vagrancy – in a duo with folk singer Wizz Jones.
item.content:encoded:
Rod Stewart has announced that his next tour will be his last.

The 81-year-old singer has been touring since the early 1960s, when he set out across Europe with a harmonica – and ended up getting deported from Spain for vagrancy – in a duo with folk singer Wizz Jones.

But while he has not ruled out one-off gigs in the future, the touring element of his career is coming to an end with Rod Stewart: The Final Encore, a tour of the UK and Europe beginning April 2027.

The arena run includes UK dates in Belfast, Glasgow, Birmingham, Manchester and London, and after an extensive European run, finishes up in Hanover, Germany, in July.

Promising “one hell of a show”, Stewart said the time has come to say farewell to life on the road. After more than six decades, The Final Encore will most definitely be his last.

He says that he has been singing the music he loves since he was 19 years old, and he has had the privilege of taking it around the world.

The rock legend says it has given him a life beyond anything he could ever have imagined, and I hope I’ve given you some fond memories in return.

Taveuni resident alleges WAF officer questioned him over speaking to media
item.description: The resident, who has asked not to be named, says the alleged incident happened a few weeks ago when he went with his team to collect water. He alleges a WAF technical officer approached him and asked why he had gone to the media about his concerns.
item.content:encoded:
The resident, who has asked not to be named, says the alleged incident happened a few weeks ago when he went with his team to collect water.

He alleges a WAF technical officer approached him and asked why he had gone to the media about his concerns.

The resident says he told the officer that it was his right to raise his concerns publicly.

He says the officer initially spoke to him in what he describes as a rough manner, but later calmed down and told him that he needed to understand the challenges WAF was facing.

fijivillage News sent questions to WAF regarding the resident's allegations.

WAF says it will look into the matter and provide a response after making the necessary enquiries.

The resident says his broader concern is that people in local communities continue to struggle for water and have to repeatedly contact WAF for assistance.

He also claims he has observed what he believes are quicker water deliveries to some hotels and expatriates, while local residents face delays.

The resident says everyone should be treated fairly and customers with WAF meters should receive proper service.

His latest concerns follow an earlier issue raised with fijivillage News over a $792 payment for 20,000 litres of water.

WAF had explained that the $792 included the cost of the water and transportation to the resident's location, with four 5,000-litre deliveries required.

The resident had said he initially received only 10,000 litres despite paying the full amount and experienced difficulty arranging delivery of the remaining water.

At the time, WAF says its Taveuni team had been waiting for the resident to contact them when he was ready to receive the remaining 10,000 litres.

fijivillage News will update the story once WAF provides a further response following its enquiries into the resident's latest allegations.
